items.title: I can describe what a gravitational field is and why it is classified as a vector field
items.what: A gravitational field is a region of space where an object with mass experiences a gravitational force. It is a vector field because at every point in space it has both a magnitude (field strength) and a direction.
items.why: Classifying the gravitational field as a vector field distinguishes it from scalar fields and allows us to represent it using arrows that show both strength and direction, which is essential for solving problems involving forces.
items.example: At a point 1000 km above Earth's surface, the gravitational field has a specific magnitude of approximately 7.3 N kg⁻¹ and is directed towards the centre of Earth. Both pieces of information are needed to fully describe the field at that point.

subtopic.name: Gravitational Field Concepts
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the definition of a gravitational field as a vector field, the distinction between uniform and non-uniform fields, and how gravitational fields are represented using field lines. It also covers the nature of mass as a gravitational monopole.
subtopic.why: Understanding gravitational fields is the foundation for all further work in this topic. The field model allows us to explain how masses exert forces on each other at a distance, and it forms the basis for understanding satellite motion and gravitational potential energy.

items.title: I can draw and interpret gravitational field line diagrams for a spherical mass
items.what: Gravitational field lines point radially inward toward the centre of a spherical mass. Lines that are closer together indicate a stronger field, and lines further apart indicate a weaker field. Field lines never cross each other.
items.why: Field line diagrams give a visual representation of how the strength and direction of gravity varies in space around a mass. Interpreting these diagrams is a required skill for both theory and exam questions.
items.example: For a diagram of Earth as a spherical mass, field lines would be drawn as arrows pointing inward from all directions toward Earth's centre. The arrows would be more densely packed close to Earth's surface and more spread out at greater distances.

subtopic.name: Gravitational Field Concepts
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the definition of a gravitational field as a vector field, the distinction between uniform and non-uniform fields, and how gravitational fields are represented using field lines. It also covers the nature of mass as a gravitational monopole.
subtopic.why: Understanding gravitational fields is the foundation for all further work in this topic. The field model allows us to explain how masses exert forces on each other at a distance, and it forms the basis for understanding satellite motion and gravitational potential energy.

items.title: I can explain why mass is described as a gravitational monopole, not a dipole
items.what: A monopole is either a pure source (field lines point outward) or a pure sink (field lines point inward). Mass is always a gravitational monopole because gravity is always attractive, so field lines always point inward toward the mass. A dipole has both a source and a sink paired together.
items.why: Understanding that gravity only attracts (never repels) explains the monopole nature of mass and distinguishes gravitational fields from magnetic and electric fields, which can form dipoles.
items.example: A bar magnet is a dipole because it has a north pole (field lines emerging) and a south pole (field lines entering). A planet like Mars has no equivalent repulsive end — its gravitational field lines all point inward, making it a monopole.

subtopic.name: Gravitational Field Concepts
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the definition of a gravitational field as a vector field, the distinction between uniform and non-uniform fields, and how gravitational fields are represented using field lines. It also covers the nature of mass as a gravitational monopole.
subtopic.why: Understanding gravitational fields is the foundation for all further work in this topic. The field model allows us to explain how masses exert forces on each other at a distance, and it forms the basis for understanding satellite motion and gravitational potential energy.

items.title: I can distinguish between uniform and non-uniform gravitational fields
items.what: A uniform gravitational field has constant strength and direction at all points, represented by evenly spaced parallel field lines. A non-uniform field varies in strength and direction, represented by field lines that are more densely packed in some regions than others.
items.why: This distinction determines which formulas and methods can be used. The formula Eg = mgΔh only applies in uniform fields, while non-uniform fields require the inverse square law or graphical methods.
items.example: Close to Earth's surface, the gravitational field can be approximated as uniform at 9.8 N kg⁻¹ downward — the field lines are approximately parallel. Further from Earth, the field is non-uniform: at 408 km altitude (the ISS), the field strength has decreased to 8.67 N kg⁻¹.

subtopic.why: Understanding gravitational fields is the foundation for all further work in this topic. The field model allows us to explain how masses exert forces on each other at a distance, and it forms the basis for understanding satellite motion and gravitational potential energy.

items.title: I can identify gravitational fields as static fields
items.what: A static field does not change over time, as opposed to a changing field that varies with time. The gravitational field around a planet is static because the mass of the planet does not change appreciably over human timescales.
items.why: Identifying whether a field is static or changing is a required classification skill in the study design and determines how the field must be modelled.
items.example: The gravitational field around Earth is considered static for calculations involving satellites and projectiles. In contrast, an electromagnetic wave involves a changing electric and magnetic field.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the definition of a gravitational field as a vector field, the distinction between uniform and non-uniform fields, and how gravitational fields are represented using field lines. It also covers the nature of mass as a gravitational monopole.
subtopic.why: Understanding gravitational fields is the foundation for all further work in this topic. The field model allows us to explain how masses exert forces on each other at a distance, and it forms the basis for understanding satellite motion and gravitational potential energy.

items.title: I can state and explain the inverse square law for gravitational fields
items.what: The gravitational field strength g is inversely proportional to the square of the distance r from the mass: g ∝ 1/r². Doubling the distance reduces the field strength to one-quarter; tripling the distance reduces it to one-ninth.
items.why: The inverse square law explains why gravity weakens with distance and allows field strength at any location to be calculated or compared without needing to know the mass of the body if a reference value is known.
items.example: At Earth's surface (r = RE), g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹. At two Earth radii from the centre (r = 2RE), g = 9.81/4 = 2.45 N kg⁻¹. At three Earth radii (r = 3RE), g = 9.81/9 = 1.09 N kg⁻¹.

subtopic.name: Inverse Square Law and Calculations
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Newton's law of universal gravitation, the inverse square law for gravitational field strength, and how to calculate gravitational field strength and gravitational force using g = GM/r² and Fg = Gm₁m₂/r².
subtopic.why: These formulas are the quantitative tools for analysing gravitational interactions at any scale — from objects on Earth's surface to satellites in orbit and planets around the Sun. They appear in almost every gravitational fields exam question.

items.title: I can calculate gravitational field strength using g = GM/r²
items.what: The gravitational field strength at a distance r from a mass M is given by g = GM/r², where G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². The variable r is measured from the centre of mass of the body, not from its surface.
items.why: This formula allows calculation of the gravitational field strength at any point around any mass, including at the surface of planets, moons, and at orbital altitudes.
items.example: To find g at the International Space Station (408 km above Earth's surface): r = (6.37 × 10⁶) + (4.08 × 10⁵) = 6.778 × 10⁶ m. Then g = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴) / (6.778 × 10⁶)² = 8.67 N kg⁻¹.

subtopic.name: Inverse Square Law and Calculations
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Newton's law of universal gravitation, the inverse square law for gravitational field strength, and how to calculate gravitational field strength and gravitational force using g = GM/r² and Fg = Gm₁m₂/r².
subtopic.why: These formulas are the quantitative tools for analysing gravitational interactions at any scale — from objects on Earth's surface to satellites in orbit and planets around the Sun. They appear in almost every gravitational fields exam question.

items.title: I can use the inverse square law ratio method to find field strength at a new distance
items.what: When the surface gravitational field strength of a body is known but its mass is not, the field strength at a new distance can be found using the ratio: g₂/g₁ = (r₁/r₂)². The mass M cancels and is not needed.
items.why: This method is efficient in exam situations where the mass of a body is not provided but the surface gravity and radii are given, such as when finding the field strength at a satellite's orbital altitude.
items.example: Mars has a surface gravity of 3.72 N kg⁻¹ and radius 3390 km. A satellite orbits at 3690 km from the centre. g_orbit = 3.72 × (3390/3690)² = 3.14 N kg⁻¹.

subtopic.name: Inverse Square Law and Calculations
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Newton's law of universal gravitation, the inverse square law for gravitational field strength, and how to calculate gravitational field strength and gravitational force using g = GM/r² and Fg = Gm₁m₂/r².
subtopic.why: These formulas are the quantitative tools for analysing gravitational interactions at any scale — from objects on Earth's surface to satellites in orbit and planets around the Sun. They appear in almost every gravitational fields exam question.

items.title: I can state Newton's law of universal gravitation and identify what each symbol represents
items.what: Newton's law of universal gravitation states that the gravitational force between two masses m₁ and m₂ separated by distance r is Fg = Gm₁m₂/r², where G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². The distance r is measured between the centres of mass of the two objects.
items.why: This law is the foundation of all gravitational force calculations and explains how gravity operates between any two masses in the universe, from apples and Earth to planets and the Sun.
items.example: Two physics students, each of mass 60 kg, sit 1.0 m apart. The gravitational force between them is F = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 60 × 60) / (1.0²) = 2.4 × 10⁻⁷ N — far too small to detect without sensitive instruments.

subtopic.name: Inverse Square Law and Calculations
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Newton's law of universal gravitation, the inverse square law for gravitational field strength, and how to calculate gravitational field strength and gravitational force using g = GM/r² and Fg = Gm₁m₂/r².
subtopic.why: These formulas are the quantitative tools for analysing gravitational interactions at any scale — from objects on Earth's surface to satellites in orbit and planets around the Sun. They appear in almost every gravitational fields exam question.

items.title: I can calculate the gravitational force acting on a mass using Fg = mg
items.what: In a known gravitational field of strength g, the gravitational force on a mass m is Fg = mg. This is equivalent to Newton's second law (F = ma) when gravity is the only force, since the acceleration equals the field strength.
items.why: This formula links the gravitational field concept (g in N kg⁻¹) to the force acting on any mass placed in that field, and directly gives the weight of an object at any location.
items.example: An astronaut of mass 80 kg standing on the Moon (g = 1.61 N kg⁻¹) experiences a gravitational force of Fg = 80 × 1.61 = 129 N, compared to 784 N on Earth's surface.

subtopic.name: Inverse Square Law and Calculations
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Newton's law of universal gravitation, the inverse square law for gravitational field strength, and how to calculate gravitational field strength and gravitational force using g = GM/r² and Fg = Gm₁m₂/r².
subtopic.why: These formulas are the quantitative tools for analysing gravitational interactions at any scale — from objects on Earth's surface to satellites in orbit and planets around the Sun. They appear in almost every gravitational fields exam question.

items.title: I can apply Newton's third law to gravitational forces between two masses
items.what: The gravitational force that mass A exerts on mass B is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force that mass B exerts on mass A. Both forces are always attractive and act along the line joining the centres of mass.
items.why: Newton's third law applied to gravity explains why both objects in a gravitational interaction accelerate toward each other, though the more massive object accelerates far less noticeably.
items.example: Earth exerts a gravitational force of approximately 2.0 × 10²⁰ N on the Moon. By Newton's third law, the Moon exerts an equal force of 2.0 × 10²⁰ N on Earth — this force causes Earth's tides.

subtopic.name: Inverse Square Law and Calculations
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Newton's law of universal gravitation, the inverse square law for gravitational field strength, and how to calculate gravitational field strength and gravitational force using g = GM/r² and Fg = Gm₁m₂/r².
subtopic.why: These formulas are the quantitative tools for analysing gravitational interactions at any scale — from objects on Earth's surface to satellites in orbit and planets around the Sun. They appear in almost every gravitational fields exam question.

items.title: I can calculate gravitational potential energy change in a uniform field using Eg = mgΔh
items.what: In a uniform gravitational field, the change in gravitational potential energy is Eg = mgΔh, where m is the mass in kg, g is the gravitational field strength in N kg⁻¹, and Δh is the change in height in metres.
items.why: This formula applies to any situation where the gravitational field can be treated as uniform — typically within a few hundred metres of a planet's surface — and is the standard method for energy calculations in projectile and motion problems.
items.example: A land diver of mass 60 kg jumps from a platform 30 m above the ground on Pentecost Island. His change in gravitational potential energy is Eg = 60 × 9.8 × 30 = 17 640 J, which is converted to kinetic energy during the fall.

subtopic.name: Gravitational Potential Energy
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers gravitational potential energy changes in uniform fields using Eg = mgΔh, qualitative understanding of potential energy changes in non-uniform fields, and how to determine changes in gravitational potential energy from the area under force–distance and field–distance graphs.
subtopic.why: Gravitational potential energy is central to energy conservation problems involving masses moving in gravitational fields. The graphical method is particularly important for objects travelling large distances where the uniform field approximation no longer holds.

items.title: I can explain why Eg = mgΔh cannot be used for large changes in height
items.what: The formula Eg = mgΔh assumes g is constant throughout the motion. As an object moves large distances away from Earth, g decreases significantly according to the inverse square law, making the constant-g assumption invalid.
items.why: Using Eg = mgΔh for large distances (such as launching a rocket to orbit) would give a significant underestimate of the energy required, because it fails to account for how gravity weakens with distance.
items.example: At Earth's surface, g ≈ 9.8 N kg⁻¹. At the altitude of the International Space Station (408 km), g ≈ 8.67 N kg⁻¹. For a rocket travelling to 10 Earth radii, g changes by a factor of 100, so Eg = mgΔh would be far too inaccurate.

subtopic.name: Gravitational Potential Energy
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers gravitational potential energy changes in uniform fields using Eg = mgΔh, qualitative understanding of potential energy changes in non-uniform fields, and how to determine changes in gravitational potential energy from the area under force–distance and field–distance graphs.
subtopic.why: Gravitational potential energy is central to energy conservation problems involving masses moving in gravitational fields. The graphical method is particularly important for objects travelling large distances where the uniform field approximation no longer holds.

items.title: I can determine the change in gravitational potential energy from the area under a force–distance graph
items.what: The change in gravitational potential energy equals the work done against gravity, which is represented by the area under a gravitational force–distance graph. For non-uniform fields, this area is estimated by counting squares on the graph.
items.why: This graphical method is the required technique for calculating potential energy changes when a mass moves through a non-uniform field, such as a spacecraft travelling to high altitude.
items.example: A force–distance graph shows a spacecraft experiencing a force decreasing from 6000 N near Earth's surface to near zero at great distance. Counting approximately 13 squares, each representing 3 × 10⁹ J, gives a total ΔEg ≈ 3.9 × 10¹⁰ J.

subtopic.name: Gravitational Potential Energy
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers gravitational potential energy changes in uniform fields using Eg = mgΔh, qualitative understanding of potential energy changes in non-uniform fields, and how to determine changes in gravitational potential energy from the area under force–distance and field–distance graphs.
subtopic.why: Gravitational potential energy is central to energy conservation problems involving masses moving in gravitational fields. The graphical method is particularly important for objects travelling large distances where the uniform field approximation no longer holds.

items.title: I can determine the change in gravitational potential energy from the area under a field–distance graph multiplied by mass
items.what: The change in gravitational potential energy can also be found by multiplying the area under a gravitational field strength–distance graph by the mass of the object. The area under the field–distance graph has units of N kg⁻¹ × m = J kg⁻¹, and multiplying by mass (kg) gives joules.
items.why: Field–distance graphs are independent of the mass of the object moving through the field, making them more versatile than force–distance graphs. The same graph can be used to find ΔEg for any mass placed in that field.
items.example: A field–distance graph for Earth shows an area of approximately 2.5 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹ between two orbital heights. For a 1200 kg space telescope, ΔEg = 2.5 × 10⁷ × 1200 = 3.0 × 10¹⁰ J.

subtopic.name: Gravitational Potential Energy
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers gravitational potential energy changes in uniform fields using Eg = mgΔh, qualitative understanding of potential energy changes in non-uniform fields, and how to determine changes in gravitational potential energy from the area under force–distance and field–distance graphs.
subtopic.why: Gravitational potential energy is central to energy conservation problems involving masses moving in gravitational fields. The graphical method is particularly important for objects travelling large distances where the uniform field approximation no longer holds.

items.title: I can qualitatively describe how gravitational potential energy changes as a mass moves in a gravitational field
items.what: Gravitational potential energy increases as a mass moves away from the centre of a gravitational body (against the direction of the field) and decreases as the mass moves toward the body (in the direction of the field). In a radial non-uniform field, potential energy increases at a decreasing rate as distance increases.
items.why: A qualitative understanding of potential energy changes is useful for reasoning about satellite motion, orbital transfers, and the energy requirements for space travel without needing detailed calculations.
items.example: A spacecraft moving from low Earth orbit to a higher geostationary orbit gains gravitational potential energy. As it continues further from Earth, the rate at which it gains potential energy decreases because the gravitational force weakens.

subtopic.name: Gravitational Potential Energy
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers gravitational potential energy changes in uniform fields using Eg = mgΔh, qualitative understanding of potential energy changes in non-uniform fields, and how to determine changes in gravitational potential energy from the area under force–distance and field–distance graphs.
subtopic.why: Gravitational potential energy is central to energy conservation problems involving masses moving in gravitational fields. The graphical method is particularly important for objects travelling large distances where the uniform field approximation no longer holds.

items.title: I can explain why the gravitational force is the centripetal force for a satellite in circular orbit
items.what: For a satellite in a stable circular orbit, gravity is the only force acting on it. This gravitational force is directed toward the centre of the orbit (the centre of the planet), which satisfies the requirement for centripetal force. Setting Fg = Fc gives the basis for all orbital calculations.
items.why: Understanding that gravity provides the centripetal force explains why satellites stay in orbit without any propulsion engines, and it is the conceptual foundation for deriving all orbital formulas.
items.example: The Moon orbits Earth because Earth's gravitational force continuously pulls the Moon toward Earth's centre. The Moon's tangential velocity is large enough that as it falls toward Earth, Earth's surface curves away at the same rate, maintaining a circular path.

subtopic.name: Orbiting Satellites
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the modelling of satellite motion as uniform circular motion, the derivation and application of formulas for orbital speed, orbital period, and orbital radius, the nature of geostationary orbits, and how to calculate the mass of a body from its satellite's motion.
subtopic.why: Satellite motion is a major application of both gravitational fields and circular motion in the VCE Physics course. These concepts underpin the technology of GPS, weather satellites, and space exploration, and orbital calculations feature in almost every exam.

items.title: I can calculate the orbital speed of a satellite using v = √(GM/r)
items.what: The orbital speed of a satellite at radius r from the centre of a body of mass M is v = √(GM/r). This formula is derived by equating gravitational force with centripetal force. Orbital speed is independent of the mass of the satellite.
items.why: This formula shows that orbital speed depends only on the mass of the central body and the orbital radius — a heavier satellite and a lighter satellite at the same altitude travel at the same speed.
items.example: The ICON satellite orbits at r = 6.97 × 10⁶ m from Earth's centre. Its orbital speed is v = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴ / 6.97 × 10⁶) = 7.56 × 10³ m s⁻¹ (approximately 7.6 km s⁻¹).

subtopic.name: Orbiting Satellites
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the modelling of satellite motion as uniform circular motion, the derivation and application of formulas for orbital speed, orbital period, and orbital radius, the nature of geostationary orbits, and how to calculate the mass of a body from its satellite's motion.
subtopic.why: Satellite motion is a major application of both gravitational fields and circular motion in the VCE Physics course. These concepts underpin the technology of GPS, weather satellites, and space exploration, and orbital calculations feature in almost every exam.

items.title: I can calculate the orbital period of a satellite using T = √(4π²r³/GM)
items.what: The orbital period T of a satellite at radius r is T = √(4π²r³/GM). This is derived from equating gravitational force with centripetal force expressed in terms of period. Like orbital speed, orbital period is independent of the satellite's mass.
items.why: The orbital period formula allows calculation of how long any satellite takes to complete one orbit, which is critical for satellite scheduling, communication windows, and understanding natural orbital systems.
items.example: The ICON satellite at r = 6.97 × 10⁶ m has an orbital period of T = √(4π² × (6.97 × 10⁶)³ / (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴)) = 5.79 × 10³ s ≈ 96.5 minutes.

subtopic.name: Orbiting Satellites
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the modelling of satellite motion as uniform circular motion, the derivation and application of formulas for orbital speed, orbital period, and orbital radius, the nature of geostationary orbits, and how to calculate the mass of a body from its satellite's motion.
subtopic.why: Satellite motion is a major application of both gravitational fields and circular motion in the VCE Physics course. These concepts underpin the technology of GPS, weather satellites, and space exploration, and orbital calculations feature in almost every exam.

items.title: I can calculate the orbital radius of a satellite using r = ³√(GMT²/4π²)
items.what: The orbital radius r of a satellite with period T orbiting a body of mass M is r = ³√(GMT²/4π²). This formula requires taking a cube root. The result gives the distance from the centre of the body, not the altitude above the surface.
items.why: Finding the orbital radius from the period is a common exam calculation, and it is used to determine the altitude required for a geostationary orbit or to verify consistency in orbital data.
items.example: To find the orbital radius of a geostationary satellite (T = 86 400 s): r = ³√(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴ × 86 400² / 4π²) = 4.2 × 10⁷ m. Altitude above surface = 4.2 × 10⁷ − 6.37 × 10⁶ ≈ 3.6 × 10⁷ m (36 000 km).

subtopic.why: Satellite motion is a major application of both gravitational fields and circular motion in the VCE Physics course. These concepts underpin the technology of GPS, weather satellites, and space exploration, and orbital calculations feature in almost every exam.

items.title: I can calculate the mass of a central body from its satellite's orbital data
items.what: Rearranging the orbital period formula gives the mass of the central body: M = 4π²r³/(GT²). By observing the orbital radius and period of any satellite, the mass of the body it orbits can be determined.
items.why: This is how astronomers determine the masses of planets, moons, and stars — by observing the motions of their natural satellites. It is also a common multi-step exam question.
items.example: Callisto orbits Jupiter with a period of 1.443 × 10⁶ s and an orbital radius of 1.883 × 10⁹ m. Mass of Jupiter = 4π² × (1.883 × 10⁹)³ / (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × (1.443 × 10⁶)²) = 1.90 × 10²⁷ kg.

items.title: I can describe the conditions required for a geostationary orbit
items.what: A geostationary satellite must orbit directly above the equator, in the same direction as Earth's rotation, and with a period of exactly 24 hours (86 400 s). All geostationary satellites are at an altitude of approximately 36 000 km above Earth's surface.
items.why: Geostationary orbits allow satellites to remain fixed above a single point on Earth's surface, making them ideal for telecommunications, weather monitoring, and broadcasting without needing to track a moving satellite.
items.example: A TV satellite dish points at a fixed position in the sky because the geostationary satellite it communicates with remains stationary relative to Earth's surface. If the satellite were in a lower orbit, it would move across the sky and the dish would need to track it.

items.title: I can predict and justify changes to orbital speed and period when orbital radius changes
items.what: As orbital radius increases, orbital speed decreases (v ∝ 1/√r) and orbital period increases (T ∝ r^(3/2)). A satellite moved to a higher orbit travels more slowly and takes longer to complete each orbit.
items.why: Understanding the relationship between orbital radius, speed, and period is essential for analysing orbital transfers and explaining why satellites at different altitudes behave differently.
items.example: A weather satellite is boosted from an altitude of 850 km to a geostationary orbit at 36 000 km. Its orbital speed decreases from approximately 7.4 km s⁻¹ to approximately 3.1 km s⁻¹, and its period increases from about 102 minutes to 24 hours.

items.title: I can distinguish between gravitational force and normal force
items.what: Gravitational force (Fg) is the attractive force exerted on a mass by a gravitational field, directed toward the centre of the gravitational body. The normal force (FN) is the contact force exerted on an object by a surface, always perpendicular to the surface. These are different forces exerted by different agents.
items.why: Confusing these two forces is a common error in exams. The gravitational force is always present in a gravitational field, while the normal force only exists when there is contact between surfaces.
items.example: A 75 kg person standing on Earth's surface experiences a downward gravitational force of Fg = 75 × 9.8 = 735 N exerted by Earth's gravitational field, and an upward normal force of FN = 735 N exerted by the floor. The net force is zero, so the person is in equilibrium.

subtopic.name: Normal Force and Apparent Weight
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the distinction between the gravitational force and the normal force, the concept of apparent weightlessness in orbiting satellites, and how to draw and interpret force diagrams for objects in gravitational fields.
subtopic.why: Understanding the difference between gravitational force and the normal force is a common source of student error. It also explains everyday phenomena such as feeling heavier in an accelerating lift and apparent weightlessness experienced by astronauts in orbit.

items.title: I can draw a force diagram showing gravitational force and normal force for an object on a surface
items.what: A force diagram for a stationary object on a horizontal surface shows two forces: the gravitational force Fg acting downward from the centre of the object, and the normal force FN acting upward from the point of contact with the surface. For a stationary object, these forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
items.why: Force diagrams are a required skill in VCE Physics and appear regularly in exams. They must use correct notation with labelled arrows showing the agent and direction of each force.
items.example: For a 20 kg box resting on a floor, draw the box as a rectangle. Add a downward arrow labelled Fg = 196 N (gravitational force exerted on box by Earth) and an upward arrow of the same length labelled FN = 196 N (normal force exerted on box by floor).

subtopic.name: Normal Force and Apparent Weight
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the distinction between the gravitational force and the normal force, the concept of apparent weightlessness in orbiting satellites, and how to draw and interpret force diagrams for objects in gravitational fields.
subtopic.why: Understanding the difference between gravitational force and the normal force is a common source of student error. It also explains everyday phenomena such as feeling heavier in an accelerating lift and apparent weightlessness experienced by astronauts in orbit.

items.title: I can explain why astronauts in an orbiting spacecraft experience apparent weightlessness
items.what: In an orbiting spacecraft, gravity is the only force acting on the astronauts and the spacecraft. Both accelerate toward Earth at the same rate (approximately 8.67 m s⁻² at the ISS altitude). Because there is no normal force (FN = 0), astronauts feel no sensation of weight and experience apparent weightlessness.
items.why: This is a widely misunderstood concept: astronauts in orbit are not outside the influence of gravity. The gravitational field at ISS altitude is 88% of that at Earth's surface. The weightlessness is apparent, not actual.
items.example: At the International Space Station (408 km altitude), the gravitational field strength is 8.67 N kg⁻¹. An astronaut of mass 80 kg experiences a gravitational force of 694 N toward Earth. They feel weightless because the ISS and astronaut are both falling toward Earth at the same rate, so no contact force is needed.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the distinction between the gravitational force and the normal force, the concept of apparent weightlessness in orbiting satellites, and how to draw and interpret force diagrams for objects in gravitational fields.
subtopic.why: Understanding the difference between gravitational force and the normal force is a common source of student error. It also explains everyday phenomena such as feeling heavier in an accelerating lift and apparent weightlessness experienced by astronauts in orbit.

items.title: I can explain that the orbital speed of a satellite is independent of the satellite's mass
items.what: When Fg = Fc is applied to derive orbital speed, the mass of the satellite m cancels from both sides of the equation, giving v = √(GM/r). This means any object at the same orbital radius will have the same orbital speed and period, regardless of its mass.
items.why: This result mirrors Galileo's observation that all objects fall at the same rate regardless of mass. It explains why a heavy and a light satellite placed in the same orbit will travel together, and why objects inside an orbiting spacecraft float freely.
items.example: A 84 kg Sputnik satellite and a 420 000 kg International Space Station, if placed at the same orbital altitude, would orbit at exactly the same speed and with the same period. The mass of the satellite has no effect on its orbital motion.
